questions.question: Your WebFlux service's event loop is stalling under load — latency spikes, some requests time out, thread dump shows event-loop threads busy. Walk through the investigation.
questions.title: Scenario — WebFlux Event Loop Stalling Under Load
questions.direct_answer: Event-loop stalls in WebFlux mean **blocking work on the wrong scheduler** — event-loop threads are sacred and must return immediately. The investigation: capture a **thread dump** during the spike to see what `reactor-http-epoll-N` threads are doing; enable **BlockHound** in non-prod to catch the culprit with a stack trace; check `reactor.netty.eventloop.pending.tasks` plus p99 latency; and audit code paths for blocking JDBC, synchronous SDKs, `Thread.sleep`, `.block()`, or CPU-heavy work on the event loop. Mitigation: wrap blocking calls with `Schedulers.boundedElastic()`, replace blocking clients with `WebClient` or R2DBC, and add circuit breakers. Long-term: consider migrating to virtual threads if the service is mostly blocking anyway.

interviewer_intent.testing: Real WebFlux production debugging, scheduler model understanding, and pragmatic prevention strategy
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding more event-loop threads, increasing timeouts, or chasing symptoms without identifying the blocking call
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss BlockHound in CI, reactor-netty metrics, scheduler isolation, degrade-gracefully patterns, and when to consider virtual threads instead

sections.title: The Symptom Pattern and What It Always Means
sections.content:
**Symptoms you'll see:**
- p99 latency spikes to seconds; p50 may still look fine
- Random timeouts on clients
- CPU modest (not saturated) but requests queue
- Thread dump shows Reactor Netty event-loop threads `RUNNABLE` inside user code (not `epollWait`)
- `reactor.netty.eventloop.pending.tasks` metric high
- Some endpoints fine, others terrible

**Root cause is almost always one of:**
- Blocking I/O on an event-loop thread (JDBC, `Thread.sleep`, synchronous HTTP client, synchronous AWS SDK)
- CPU-heavy synchronous code on the event loop (JSON parsing on huge payloads, crypto, compression)
- `.block()` called inside the reactive chain
- A `synchronized` block holding a lock while doing I/O
- A deep call into a legacy library that happens to be blocking

Reactor Netty defaults to `2 × CPU` event-loop threads. If a handler takes 500 ms of CPU or blocks on I/O, **each event-loop thread can only serve 2 requests/sec** — across all requests. Latency balloons; the queue grows.

The fix is *never* "add more event-loop threads." That masks the real problem and wastes memory.

sections.title: Where Blocking Sneaks Into a Reactive Chain
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    req[Request] --> el["Netty event-loop thread (4-8 total)"]
    el --> ctl[Controller]
    ctl --> a["WebClient call (non-blocking OK)"]
    ctl --> b["jdbcTemplate.query BLOCKING on event-loop"]
    ctl --> c["R2DBC query non-blocking OK"]
    ctl --> d["Synchronous AWS SDK BLOCKING"]
    ctl --> e["CompletableFuture.get BLOCKING"]
    ctl --> f[".block() call deadlock risk"]
    b -.stalls event loop.-> stall["Other requests queue behind"]
    d -.stalls event loop.-> stall
    e -.stalls event loop.-> stall
    f -.stalls event loop.-> stall
```

sections.title: Step 1 — Immediate Diagnosis
sections.content:
Collect data while the spike is happening — guessing afterwards is much harder.

**Capture three thread dumps 10 seconds apart**
- Multiple samples reveal patterns vs one-off snapshots
- Use `jstack` or Spring Boot Actuator

```bash
jstack <pid> > thread-dump-1.txt
sleep 10
jstack <pid> > thread-dump-2.txt
sleep 10
jstack <pid> > thread-dump-3.txt
```

Or via Actuator: `GET /actuator/threaddump`.

**Identify event-loop threads**
- Named `reactor-http-epoll-N` (Linux / epoll) or `reactor-http-nio-N`
- These should be in `epollWait` between requests

**Read the stack frames**
- `RUNNABLE` inside `jdbc`, `SqlDriver.execute`, `java.net.SocketInputStream.read` — blocking I/O
- `RUNNABLE` inside JSON / XML parsing or crypto — CPU-bound
- `WAITING` on `LockSupport.park` or `Object.wait` — deadlock or contention
- `RUNNABLE` inside `EpollEventLoop.run` — healthy idle state

**A healthy event-loop thread stack**

```
reactor-http-epoll-3 RUNNABLE
    at io.netty.channel.epoll.Native.epollWait0(Native Method)
    at io.netty.channel.epoll.EpollEventLoop.epollWait(...)
    at io.netty.channel.epoll.EpollEventLoop.run(...)
```

**An UNHEALTHY one**

```
reactor-http-epoll-3 RUNNABLE
    at java.net.SocketInputStream.read(...)
    at com.mysql.cj.protocol.StandardSocketFactory.connect(...)
    at com.myapp.OrderService.fetchOrder(OrderService.java:45)
    at ...Controller...
```

Blocking JDBC on an event-loop thread — there's your culprit.

**Capture key metrics during the spike**
- `reactor.netty.eventloop.pending.tasks` — work backing up
- `jvm.threads.states{state="runnable"}`
- `http.server.requests` p50, p95, p99
- JVM CPU %
- GC pause time (G1 / ZGC)
- `reactor.netty.connection.provider.acquire.time` for outbound calls

**Application logs**
- Slow query warnings
- Timeout errors
- GC logs

sections.title: Step 2 — Confirm with BlockHound in Non-Prod
sections.content:
**BlockHound** is a JVM agent that throws if it sees blocking calls on non-blocking schedulers. It pinpoints the exact stack frame at fault.

**Install in non-prod or canary**

```java
@PostConstruct
void blockHound() {
    if (environment.acceptsProfiles("dev", "staging")) {
        BlockHound.install();
    }
}
```

Or via agent: `-javaagent:blockhound-agent.jar`.

**What you'll see**

```
reactor.blockhound.BlockingOperationError: Blocking call! jdbc:postgresql
    at java.base/java.net.SocketInputStream.read(...)
    at com.mysql.cj.protocol.NetworkResource.read(...)
    at com.myapp.orders.OrderRepository.findById(OrderRepository.java:28)
    at com.myapp.orders.OrderService.lambda$findById$0(OrderService.java:19)
```

**Reproduce under controlled load**
- Use k6, Gatling, or vegeta to hit the service
- Correlate spikes with BlockHound errors and slow query logs
- Confirm your hypothesis before rolling a fix

**Why staging not production**
- BlockHound throws on every offending call — it's noisy
- A canary instance gives you signal without taking down prod

sections.title: Step 3 — Fix Categories
Step 4 — Prevent and Monitor
sections.content:
**Observability metrics**
- `reactor.netty.eventloop.pending.tasks` — alert if greater than 100 for 1 minute
- `jvm.threads.states{state="blocked"}` — spike indicates contention
- `http.server.requests` p99 per endpoint
- `reactor.netty.connection.provider.acquire.time`
- `executor.queued` on the `boundedElastic` scheduler

**Dashboards**
- p99 latency per endpoint
- Event-loop pending tasks
- Active connections per pool
- Slow queries (DB-side)
- GC pause histogram

**Alerts**
- p99 over 2x baseline for 5 minutes
- Event-loop pending greater than 100
- BlockHound errors in staging
- R2DBC / HTTP pool exhaustion

**Prevention practices**
- **Mandatory BlockHound in staging CI** — load tests run against staged builds with BlockHound enabled
- **Lint for `.block()`** — ArchUnit rule banning `.block()` in reactive-module packages
- **Code review checklist** — any blocking library, `synchronized` with I/O, blocking `java.net.Socket`
- **`boundedElastic` budget** — configure `max-threads`; monitor saturation

**Degrade gracefully under load**
- Rate limiter (Resilience4j) at entry — shed excess load
- Bulkhead to isolate slow dependencies
- Circuit breaker around every external call
- Timeout on every `WebClient` / R2DBC call
- Fallback for non-critical data — cached, stale-but-OK

**Architectural alternatives**
- If the service is mostly blocking work, migrate to **Spring MVC + virtual threads** — simpler code, no event loop to stall
- If latency-sensitive with genuinely async upstream, keep WebFlux and fix the blocking hot paths

**Capacity planning**
- CPU cores × 2 = event-loop threads — handle thousands of concurrent I/O
- `boundedElastic` default unlimited; configure bound for heavy use
- Connection pools (R2DBC, WebClient) must match DB / upstream capacity
- Run load tests at 1.5x peak; find the breakpoint before production does

**Post-mortem questions** - Why wasn't the blocking call caught earlier?
- (no BlockHound? no code review?)
- How do we prevent regression?
- (lint rule, test, runtime check)
- Is monitoring sufficient to detect this in the future?
- (event-loop pending alert)
- Should we migrate to virtual threads?
- (if reactive benefits aren't paying off)

sections.title: Hard-Earned Lessons and Investigation Checklist
sections.content:
**Lessons from production WebFlux work:**
- **Reactive is not self-protecting** — synchronous code in a reactive handler isn't caught by the framework; you need tooling and discipline
- **Mixing blocking and reactive is fragile** — the worst failure modes come from 1% of requests on a blocking path stalling shared event-loop threads
- **More threads is not the fix** — it's tempting to bump `reactor.netty.ioWorkerCount`; this masks the real problem
- **`boundedElastic` has limits** — default `10 × CPU`, max queue 100K; pushing too much blocking work there exhausts it
- **`@Transactional` in reactive** needs `R2dbcTransactionManager`; thread-local tx won't work across the chain
- **Timeouts everywhere** — every outbound call needs explicit `timeout()`; without it, a slow upstream stalls indefinitely
- **Backpressure at ingress** — a fast client can overwhelm a slow backend; rate limit at the edge
- **Async-profiler / JFR** for reactive — sampling profilers may miss short-lived blocks
- **Know your scheduler** — `subscribeOn` first wins, `publishOn` switches downstream
- **Consider Project Loom** — if you keep wrapping with `boundedElastic`, ask whether the service should be reactive at all

**The investigation checklist:** 1.
- Thread dump — identify event-loop threads, what they're doing
2.
- Metrics — pending tasks, p99 latency, pool saturation
3.
- BlockHound in staging — confirm blocking call with stack trace
4.
- Classify — JDBC, sync SDK, CPU-heavy, `.block()`?
5.
- Fix — wrap with `boundedElastic`, migrate to reactive client, hop to `parallel()`, redesign
6.
- Verify — rerun load test, watch metrics
7.
- Prevent — BlockHound in CI, code review rules, monitoring alerts
8.
- Reflect — should this service be reactive at all, or is MVC + virtual threads better?

**One-line summary**
- Event-loop stalls in WebFlux are blocking code on the wrong scheduler
- Find it with BlockHound and thread dumps
- Move blocking work to `boundedElastic` or replace with reactive alternatives
- Prevent regressions with tooling
- Consider virtual threads if the service isn't genuinely reactive

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Event-loop stalls = blocking code on a non-blocking scheduler**
- **Thread dump** identifies the culprit — `reactor-http-epoll-N` threads stuck in user code
- **BlockHound** pinpoints blocking calls with stack traces in non-prod
- **Key metrics** — `reactor.netty.eventloop.pending.tasks`, p99 latency, pool saturation
- **Common culprits** — JDBC, sync SDKs, `Thread.sleep`, `.block()`, CPU-heavy sync, `synchronized` with I/O
- **Fix** — wrap with `subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())`, migrate to reactive client, or hop to `parallel()`
- **Never** fix by adding more event-loop threads
- **Prevent** — BlockHound in staging CI, lint rules, code review, monitoring alerts
- **Degrade gracefully** — rate limiters, bulkheads, circuit breakers, fallbacks
- **Consider MVC + virtual threads** if the service is mostly blocking anyway

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Event-loop stalls in WebFlux mean blocking work on the wrong scheduler — event-loop threads must return immediately.

**Symptom pattern**
- p99 spikes to seconds; p50 maybe OK
- Random timeouts; CPU modest but requests queue
- Thread dump shows `reactor-http-epoll-N` threads `RUNNABLE` in user code, not `epollWait`
- `reactor.netty.eventloop.pending.tasks` high

**Step 1 — Diagnose**
- Three thread dumps 10s apart
- Identify event-loop threads (`reactor-http-epoll-N`)
- Read the frames — JDBC / `SocketInputStream.read` = blocking I/O; JSON / crypto = CPU; `LockSupport.park` = contention
- Capture metrics — pending tasks, p99, pool saturation, GC pauses

**Step 2 — Confirm with BlockHound in non-prod**
- JVM agent throws on blocking calls on non-blocking schedulers
- Install only on dev / staging profile
- Reproduce under load with k6 / Gatling; correlate spikes with BlockHound errors

**Step 3 — Fix categories**
- Blocking JDBC — `Mono.fromCallable(...).subscribeOn(boundedElastic())` or migrate to R2DBC
- Synchronous HTTP — replace `RestTemplate` with `WebClient`
- Synchronous SDKs — AWS v2 async + `Mono.fromFuture`
- CPU-heavy — `publishOn(Schedulers.parallel())`
- `.block()` in chain — replace with `flatMap`
- `synchronized` with I/O — fetch outside lock; use `ReentrantLock` or `putIfAbsent`
- Bulk work on one thread — `flatMap(fn, 32)` or `parallel().runOn(parallel())`

**Step 4 — Prevent and monitor**
- Metrics — `reactor.netty.eventloop.pending.tasks`, p99 per endpoint
- Alerts — pending greater than 100; p99 2x baseline; BlockHound errors
- BlockHound mandatory in staging CI
- ArchUnit lint banning `.block()` in reactive packages
- Degrade gracefully — rate limiter, bulkhead, circuit breaker, timeouts, fallbacks

**Hard-earned lessons**
- Reactive is not self-protecting; tooling and discipline are required
- Mixing blocking and reactive is fragile
- More threads is not the fix
- `boundedElastic` has limits — don't push everything blocking there
- Timeouts on every outbound call
- Consider MVC + virtual threads if you keep wrapping blocking calls

**The one-line summary**
- Event-loop stalls are blocking code on the wrong scheduler
- Find with BlockHound and thread dumps
- Move to `boundedElastic` or replace with reactive alternatives
- Prevent with tooling
- Consider virtual threads if reactive isn't paying off

questions.question: A downstream HTTP service your WebFlux app depends on starts degrading — p99 climbs from 50ms to 5s. Your service starts dropping requests because of pool exhaustion. Walk through the mitigation.
questions.title: Scenario — Degrading Upstream and Cascading Failure
questions.direct_answer: When a slow upstream eats your `WebClient` connection pool, every request waiting on that upstream piles up in `pendingAcquireQueue` and the whole service degrades. The mitigation has four layers: tight **per-call timeouts** so requests fail fast rather than wait forever; a **circuit breaker** (Resilience4j) that opens after a failure threshold and short-circuits subsequent calls; a **bulkhead** that caps concurrent calls to the failing upstream so it can't starve other workloads; and a **fallback** — cached value, default response, or queued retry. Long-term: split clients per upstream so one slow dependency can't poison shared pools, and design endpoints to **degrade gracefully** with partial responses.

interviewer_intent.testing: Production hygiene around external dependencies, resilience patterns, and the cascading-failure failure mode of WebFlux pools
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Increasing pool size to 'absorb' the slowness; missing the bulkhead concept; treating retries as a fix when they amplify the problem
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss per-upstream pool isolation, circuit breaker half-open probing, queueing-theory intuition for pendingAcquireQueue, and graceful degradation patterns

sections.title: How a Slow Upstream Becomes a Service-Wide Outage
sections.content:
**The cascading-failure pattern is universal.** A downstream service's p99 climbs from 50 ms to 5 seconds.
- Your service still tries to call it on every request.
- Each in-flight call holds one connection from the upstream pool.
- As more requests arrive, the pool fills, and new requests wait in `pendingAcquireQueue`.
- Eventually that queue fills too — at which point requests start failing with `PoolAcquireTimeoutException` and the entire service appears down, even for endpoints that don't depend on the slow upstream.

**Why WebFlux makes this worse than MVC**
- A few event-loop threads serve thousands of in-flight calls
- A slow upstream consumes connection-pool slots, not threads
- The queue grows quietly until it overflows
- Without explicit bulkheads, one slow upstream can poison everything

The defense is **layered resilience** — per-call timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, fallbacks, and isolated client pools. None of these alone is enough; together they convert a shared-failure pattern into a contained one.

sections.title: Pool Exhaustion Cascade
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    inc["Incoming requests (5K/s)"] --> ctl[Controller]
    ctl --> wc["WebClient (one shared pool of 50)"]
    wc --> up1["Upstream A (healthy 50ms)"]
    wc --> up2["Upstream B SLOW (5s p99)"]
    up2 -.connections held.-> wc
    wc -.queue grows.-> q["pendingAcquireQueue exhausted"]
    q --> err["PoolAcquireTimeoutException"]
    err -.affects.-> up1Calls["Even calls to A start failing"]
```

sections.title: Step 1 — Tight Per-Call Timeouts
sections.content:
Every outbound call needs an explicit timeout. Defaults are too long or absent.

**Configure at the `WebClient` level**
- `responseTimeout` covers the full response cycle
- `ChannelOption.CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MILLIS` covers TCP connect
- `ReadTimeoutHandler` and `WriteTimeoutHandler` cover individual frames

```java
HttpClient http = HttpClient.create(connectionProvider)
    .responseTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
    .option(ChannelOption.CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MILLIS, 1000)
    .doOnConnected(c -> c
        .addHandlerLast(new ReadTimeoutHandler(2))
        .addHandlerLast(new WriteTimeoutHandler(2)));

WebClient client = WebClient.builder()
    .clientConnector(new ReactorClientHttpConnector(http))
    .build();
```

**Per-call timeout for tighter control**

```java
client.get().uri("/slow")
    .retrieve()
    .bodyToMono(Result.class)
    .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(500));
```

**Why this matters**
- A request that times out in 500 ms releases its connection back to the pool
- A request that waits 5 seconds holds its slot the whole time
- Tight timeouts are the single biggest lever against pool exhaustion

**Don't pick timeouts arbitrarily**
- Choose based on upstream's healthy p99 plus a buffer
- If healthy p99 is 100 ms, set timeout to 300-500 ms
- Anything longer means you're tolerating degradation

sections.title: Step 2 — Circuit Breaker (Resilience4j)
sections.content:
A circuit breaker opens after a failure threshold and short-circuits subsequent calls — failing immediately instead of waiting on a known-broken upstream.

**Three states**
- **Closed** — normal operation, calls pass through
- **Open** — calls fail immediately without reaching upstream
- **Half-open** — after a wait, allow limited probe calls; if they succeed, close; if they fail, open again

**Resilience4j configuration**

```java
CircuitBreakerConfig config = CircuitBreakerConfig.custom()
    .failureRateThreshold(50)
    .slowCallRateThreshold(50)
    .slowCallDurationThreshold(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
    .slidingWindowType(SlidingWindowType.COUNT_BASED)
    .slidingWindowSize(20)
    .minimumNumberOfCalls(10)
    .waitDurationInOpenState(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
    .permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState(3)
    .build();

CircuitBreaker cb = CircuitBreaker.of("upstream-b", config);
```

**Wire into a reactive chain**

```java
return webClient.get().uri("/b/data").retrieve().bodyToMono(Data.class)
    .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(500))
    .transformDeferred(CircuitBreakerOperator.of(cb))
    .onErrorResume(CallNotPermittedException.class,
        ex -> Mono.just(Data.fallback()));
```

**Effect**
- During the upstream incident, calls fail fast in microseconds
- The pool stops getting consumed
- The rest of your service stays healthy
- After 30 seconds, half-open lets 3 probe calls through; if upstream recovered, traffic resumes

sections.title: Step 3 — Bulkhead and Per-Upstream Pool Isolation
sections.content:
**Bulkhead** caps concurrent calls to a single upstream so it can't consume the entire pool.

**Resilience4j BulkheadOperator**

```java
BulkheadConfig bulkConfig = BulkheadConfig.custom()
    .maxConcurrentCalls(20)
    .maxWaitDuration(Duration.ofMillis(50))
    .build();

Bulkhead bulkhead = Bulkhead.of("upstream-b", bulkConfig);

return webClient.get().uri("/b/data").retrieve().bodyToMono(Data.class)
    .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(500))
    .transformDeferred(BulkheadOperator.of(bulkhead))
    .transformDeferred(CircuitBreakerOperator.of(cb))
    .onErrorResume(BulkheadFullException.class,
        ex -> Mono.just(Data.fallback()));
```

**Per-upstream `WebClient` beans — pool isolation**
- The deepest bulkhead is a separate connection pool per upstream
- One slow upstream can't starve calls to another

```java
@Bean("clientB")
public WebClient clientB() {
    HttpClient http = HttpClient.create(ConnectionProvider.builder("poolB")
            .maxConnections(40)
            .pendingAcquireMaxCount(80)
            .pendingAcquireTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(100))
            .build())
        .responseTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2));
    return WebClient.builder()
        .baseUrl("https://b.internal")
        .clientConnector(new ReactorClientHttpConnector(http))
        .build();
}
```

**Why pool isolation matters most**
- Without it, every shared client uses one pool — slow upstream eats it for everyone
- With separate pools, the blast radius shrinks to just the affected upstream
- This is the single most impactful architectural change for resilience

sections.title: Step 4 — Fallback and Graceful Degradation
sections.content:
When you can't reach the upstream, return *something* useful instead of failing.

**Cached value as fallback**

```java
return webClient.get().uri("/b/recommendations").retrieve().bodyToFlux(Reco.class)
    .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(500))
    .transformDeferred(CircuitBreakerOperator.of(cb))
    .onErrorResume(ex -> {
        log.warn("upstream-b unavailable, serving cached", ex);
        return cacheClient.getCachedRecommendations(userId);
    });
```

**Default / static fallback**

```java
.onErrorResume(ex -> Mono.just(Recommendations.empty()))
```

**Partial response composition**
- An endpoint that aggregates several upstreams should return what it could fetch
- Mark missing pieces explicitly in the response so clients can degrade their UI

```java
public Mono<UserDashboard> dashboard(String userId) {
    return Mono.zip(
        profileService.fetch(userId).onErrorReturn(Profile.empty()),
        ordersService.fetch(userId).onErrorReturn(List.of()),
        recsService.fetch(userId).onErrorReturn(List.of()))
        .map(t -> new UserDashboard(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3()));
}
```

**What NOT to do**
- Don't blanket-retry on a failing upstream — you amplify load on something already broken
- Don't increase the pool size to "absorb" slowness — the queue just grows bigger
- Don't return generic 5xx for partial-failure cases — clients can often handle partial data better

**Retry with care**
- Only retry idempotent operations
- Use exponential backoff with jitter
- Cap retries small (2-3)
- Combine with circuit breaker so retries stop when upstream is known broken

sections.title: What Helps, What Hurts, and How to Tune
sections.content:
**When the stack helps:**
- Tight timeouts release connections so they don't accumulate
- Circuit breakers fail fast during incidents, sparing the pool and the upstream
- Bulkheads cap the blast radius of any one failing upstream
- Pool isolation per upstream prevents shared-pool starvation
- Fallbacks turn outages into degraded but useful responses

**When patterns hurt:**
- Timeouts too tight — false-positive failures on healthy upstreams under brief load
- Circuit breaker too sensitive — flips open on noise; configure `minimumNumberOfCalls` carefully
- Bulkhead too small — caps healthy throughput; tune to actual concurrent need
- Fallbacks that mask real failures — without metrics, you don't notice the upstream is broken
- Retries without circuit breaker — amplify load on a struggling upstream

**Watch for:**
- **Pool exhaustion masking the real issue** — `PoolAcquireTimeoutException` looks like a network bug; the real cause is upstream slowness consuming connections
- **`pendingAcquireMaxCount` defaults** — set explicit values so the queue can't grow unbounded
- **One shared `WebClient` for everything** — biggest source of cascading failures; split per upstream
- **Retries on non-idempotent writes** — duplicate side effects without idempotency keys
- **Missing observability** — circuit breaker state, bulkhead rejections, fallback rates must be on dashboards

**Tuning rules of thumb:**
- Timeout = upstream healthy p99 × 3-5
- `maxConnections` = expected concurrent need plus 20% headroom
- `pendingAcquireMaxCount` = `maxConnections × 2` plus a small queue
- `pendingAcquireTimeout` short — 100-500 ms; fail fast over wait long
- Circuit breaker threshold — 50% failure rate over a 20-call window with at least 10 calls
- Bulkhead `maxConcurrentCalls` — match upstream's published capacity, not your service's load

**Observability essentials:**
- `resilience4j.circuitbreaker.state` per name — alert on Open
- `resilience4j.bulkhead.available.concurrent.calls`
- `reactor.netty.connection.provider.acquire.time` per pool
- `http.client.requests` p99 per upstream
- Fallback invocation rate per endpoint — if non-zero, something's degraded

**Strategic guidance**
- Treat external dependencies as adversarial — they will degrade and you must contain it
- Per-upstream pool isolation is the highest-leverage architectural change
- Combine timeouts, circuit breaker, bulkhead, and fallback — none alone is enough
- Test failure modes in chaos exercises, not just under load
- Make degradation visible — partial responses with explicit "unavailable" markers are better than blanket 5xx

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Cascading failure** — slow upstream fills the pool, queue grows, the whole service degrades
- **Per-call timeouts** are the single biggest lever; without them, slow calls hold connections forever
- **Circuit breaker (Resilience4j)** opens after failure threshold and short-circuits broken upstream
- **Bulkhead** caps concurrent calls so one upstream can't starve others
- **Per-upstream pool isolation** is the highest-leverage architectural change
- **Fallback** — cached value, default, partial response — turns outage into degraded service
- **Don't increase pool size** to absorb slowness — the queue just grows
- **Don't blanket-retry** on failing upstream — amplifies load
- **Tight `pendingAcquireTimeout`** — fail fast over wait long
- **Observability** — circuit breaker state, bulkhead rejections, fallback rate must alert
- **Test failure modes** in chaos exercises, not just under load

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
When a slow upstream eats your `WebClient` connection pool, every request piles up in `pendingAcquireQueue` and the service degrades. The mitigation is layered.

**Layer 1 — Tight per-call timeouts**
- `responseTimeout`, connect timeout, read / write timeout on the `HttpClient`
- Per-call `timeout(Duration)` in the chain
- Pick based on upstream healthy p99 — typically 3-5x
- A request that times out fast releases its connection

**Layer 2 — Circuit breaker (Resilience4j)**
- Three states — Closed, Open, Half-open
- Configure failure-rate threshold, slow-call threshold, sliding window, half-open probe count
- Wire into the chain via `CircuitBreakerOperator`
- During incident, calls fail fast in microseconds; pool stops getting consumed

**Layer 3 — Bulkhead and pool isolation**
- Resilience4j Bulkhead caps concurrent calls
- Deeper bulkhead — a separate `WebClient` bean per upstream with its own connection pool
- Single most impactful architectural change for resilience

**Layer 4 — Fallback**
- Cached value, static default, partial response
- `Mono.zip` with `onErrorReturn` per dependency for graceful degradation
- Mark missing pieces in response; clients can degrade their UI

**What NOT to do**
- Don't blanket-retry — amplifies load on broken upstream
- Don't increase pool size to absorb — queue just grows bigger
- Don't return generic 5xx for partial-failure cases — clients can handle partial data

**Tuning rules of thumb**
- Timeout — upstream healthy p99 × 3-5
- `pendingAcquireTimeout` — 100-500 ms
- Circuit breaker — 50% failure rate over 20 calls minimum 10
- Bulkhead — match upstream capacity, not your load

**Observability essentials**
- Circuit breaker state per upstream — alert on Open
- Bulkhead available concurrent calls
- Pool acquire time per pool
- Fallback invocation rate — non-zero means degradation

**Strategic answer**
- Treat external dependencies as adversarial — they will degrade
- Per-upstream pool isolation is the highest-leverage change
- Combine timeouts, circuit breaker, bulkhead, fallback — none alone is enough
- Test failure modes in chaos exercises
- Make degradation visible with partial responses, not blanket 5xx
